Subscribe to enjoy similar stories . <p> This World Population Day , let us critique the proposition that population growth is inherently bad for the planet . The notion that more people inevitably means more emissions , higher degradation and a greater drain on resources is arguably one-sided and might obscure where real solutions lie . <p> India , now the world 's most populous country , sits at the confluence of two big shifts : climate vulnerability and demographic opportunity . Could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advantage ? What we do with our population and not just how many we are will shape not only India 's future , but also the world 's climate trajectory . <p> A global population puzzle : Population trends are disparate . Many countries -- like China , Japan and some in Europe -- are wrestling with falling birth rates and ageing populations . There is an increasing chorus actively encouraging citizens to have more children . <p> At the same time , quite a few entire nations or specific population segments still contend with large family sizes and poor access to reproductive healthcare . The dilemma here is not the number of people alone , but their agency and access to planned parenthood -- choices shaped by societal norms , education , healthcare , financial independence and physical access , plus the affordability of birth control . <p> So , yes , population still matters . But not in the shrill tones sometimes employed . It matters because well-being , equity and sustainability are interwoven , and that 's where India 's size and scale come to the fore @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : India 's population of over 1.4 billion is often seen as a challenge . But our size is also a powerful handle . It enables climate solutions to be deployed at costs and speeds that smaller nations simply can not match . Whether it 's electric mobility , distributed renewables or climate-resilient agriculture , if India gets it right , it would shift global economics , trajectories and expectations . <p> This is already happening . Today , India leads the world in solar irrigation , energy-efficient lighting and electric two- as well as three-wheelers . These gains did n't occur despite our population , but because of it . <p> Vulnerability as a catalyst : Indian demography is young , mobile and increasingly urban . These dimensions create pressures , but also gameness for change . Unlike older economies with deep-set infrastructure , India has the conditions and will to become the first major economy to industrialize without carbonizing . This would mean leapfrogging to cleaner , more efficient systems -- low-carbon cities , resilient agriculture and a skilled green workforce . <p> At the same time , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more frequent and severe . The vulnerability is real . But that urgency also fuels innovation . Some of India 's most promising climate solutions are emerging not from boardrooms , but from communities on the front lines of change . <p> Our population can drive climate action : India has the natural resources to grow and thrive , whether it is to grow all the food we must or to generate all the renewables we need . However , we do also require a step change in resource efficiency and productivity -- higher yields , better incomes and lower environmental impact . From green cooling technologies to sustainable construction materials , India 's scale generates the addressable market size to commercialize solutions that can lower the ' green premium ' for India and potentially for the rest of the world too . <p> Having said all this , population is non-discriminating ; it can amplify both our strengths and weaknesses . To turn it into a climate asset , we must invest in the foundational building blocks that still need strength : education , healthcare , skilling , female @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy frameworks . <p> Scale across the board : India 's population is not a uniform monolith . A climate strategy that ignores inequality wo n't just be unfair , it will be ineffective . <p> Ensuring that those who are most vulnerable to climate stress are afforded the ability to adapt has to be a critical foundation of our climate strategy . A recent policy brief by the Asian Development Bank ( ADB ) , supported by the Japan Fund for Prosperous and Resilient Asia and the Pacific , explores how the country is navigating this complex issue . The study benefits from inputs from institutions like the International Centre for Climate Change and Development ( ICCCAD ) , UN Women Bangladesh , and key government ministries . With increasing climate-related disasters threatening its densely populated and vulnerable terrain , Bangladesh has developed a legal and policy framework that embeds gender sensitivity into disaster governance . This evolution reflects both domestic constitutional mandates and international commitments , yet gaps in implementation and representation reveal that the journey is still far from complete . <h> When Disasters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- Brahmaputra Delta leaves it especially vulnerable to floods , cyclones , river erosion , and droughts . These inequalities become life-threatening during emergencies , where caregiving responsibilities constrain their ability to evacuate and access relief services . The cumulative effect is a cycle of vulnerability that requires a systemic and inclusive policy response . <p> Yet , Bangladesh has not stood still . The Disaster Management Act of 2012 laid the foundation for a structured @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of ensuring gender representation in high-level decision-making bodies such as the National Disaster Management Council ( NDMC ) . Articles 40 and 42 guarantee occupational freedom and property rights , two areas that have direct relevance in post-disaster recovery . These constitutional provisions set the legal precedent for integrating gender equity across all spheres of public policy , including climate adaptation and disaster management . <p> International frameworks further reinforce these principles . Bangladesh is a signatory to the Paris Agreement and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ( UNFCCC ) , both of which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction , whose Gender Action Plan ( Sendai GAP ) outlines a roadmap for integrating gender into risk management . Although Bangladesh maintains reservations about certain provisions of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women ( CEDAW ) , it has nevertheless adopted many of its recommendations in national law and policy . In particular , CEDAW 's General Recommendation No. 37 urges governments to integrate gender dimensions in DRM and climate responses . <h> Policies in Practice : Moving Beyond Rhetoric <p> On the domestic front , several policy instruments reflect Bangladesh 's growing commitment to gender equity . It aims not only to mitigate inequalities but to transform systems and outcomes through gender-responsive climate governance . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ also emphasizes women 's participation and targets the unique vulnerabilities of children , the elderly , and persons with disabilities . While the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act of 1995 remains largely gender-neutral , its broad scope allows other policies , like the 2016 Gender Policy , to address gender inclusion in areas like flood control and environmental sustainability . The post-pandemic period has prompted the ruling governments in India to adopt a more sensible approach . They are now focusing on a strategy that emphasises setting targets to revive the slowing economy and align it with sustainable development goals . This strategy particularly aims to promote resource efficiency and responsible production and consumption practices , steering the economy back onto a path of rapid growth . <p> Although the world has been actively discussing and debating ways to achieve sustainable development and implementing various action plans at different levels , the importance of integrating mindful consumption and production is rarely highlighted despite its inclusion in the Sustainable Development Goals ( SDGs ) . Recognising the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ essential . This approach aims to minimise the environmental impact of our consumption and production patterns by using resources efficiently and consciously , reducing waste , and promoting best practices throughout the production cycle . It ensures that current needs are met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs -- essentially " doing more with less " while mitigating climate change and preserving ecosystems . This process wo n't be an easily achievable one for a developing country like India for the following reasons . <p> According to an update from the World Economic Forum , India is expected to become one of the largest consumer markets in the world by 2030 . The urban population in India is projected to double , reaching 800 million by 2050 ( UN DESA , 2018a ) , accompanied by a more than 300% increase in per capita GDP ( PwC , 2017 ) . This rising urban population and increasing income levels will intensify the challenges related to the unsustainable consumption of resources , including energy and materials . For instance , India 's share of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from 6.1% in 2017 to 9.1% by 2030 . Moreover , India 's energy demand may double by 2040 , driven by the growing ownership of appliances and a rising need for cooling ( IEA , 2020 ) . Energy is not the only resource being depleted at an unsustainable rate ; the construction sector also accounts for a significant portion of India 's material consumption . Each year , India consumes between 1,200 and 1,300 million tons of construction minerals ( BMTPC , 2018 ; Ministry of Mines , 2018 ) . Due to significant shortages , India has begun importing certain construction minerals , especially sand , from other countries ( Kukreti , 2018 ) . <p> Energy and waste management are two prominent streams facilitating resource efficiency and the country 's transition to Sustainable Consumption and Production ( SCP ) . India generates between 100 and 300 Mt of construction and demolition waste ( C&amp;DW ) annually ( Jain et al. , 2018 ) , but a major fraction of the waste is either openly dumped or landfilled , which increases human health risks , land-use conflicts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Joshi &amp; Ahmed , 2016 ) . Greater electrification and changing living standards have led to higher electricity demand in India , and trends are expected to continue with the electrification of the economy and grid connections for all households ( MoSPI , 2017 ) . The building sector in India contributes to the consumption of about 33% of the total energy produced , of which the residential sector consumes 24% and 9% by the commercial sector . Additionally , increasing prosperity levels and shifting cultural trends ( consumption-based society ) in India have led to the purchase and use of a large number of electrical and electronic appliances across households , offices , and industries . Both factors contributed to India 's rise in total and per capita electricity consumption ( CEA , 2018 ) . <p> Indian governments launched different policies intending to manage energy efficiency in the electricity and construction sectors . The Energy Conservation Act 2001 deserve special mention in this matter . This Act was first made applicable only for large commercial buildings but was updated in 2010 to include smaller ones . Under this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2007 was created to improve energy efficiency , though following it was initially optional . Because few people followed it , ECBC 2017 made it mandatory for commercial buildings to save at least 25% energy . More savings can earn ECBC Plus or Super ECBC labels . HVAC systems ( heating , ventilation , and air conditioning ) use 55% of the total energy in commercial buildings . The Standards &amp; Labelling ( S&amp;L ) Scheme ( 2006 ) sets minimum energy efficiency rules for appliances . <p> In homes , energy efficiency rules are not strongly followed . The Eco-Niwas initiative ( 2018 ) was launched to improve this , along with older programs like BEE 's Star Labelling and UJALA ( 2015 ) , which promote LED bulbs . As these materials are non-renewable , increasing demand may lead to resource shortages and environmental damage . Some minerals are already scarce , and India has even started importing sand due to sand shortages . A possible solution is recycling construction and demolition waste ( C&amp;DW ) , one of India 's fastest-growing waste types . Estimates suggest that urban areas generate up to 700 million tons of C&amp;DW annually . However , India lacks a proper waste management system . Most C&amp;DW is mixed with regular waste and dumped in cities . Only a small portion , such as whole bricks and valuable materials , is resold , while the rest is sent to landfills or dumped openly . Recycling C&amp;DW can help reduce raw material demand , free up land , and reduce environmental harm . It also creates jobs and attracts investment . Promoting resource efficiency and a circular economy in construction @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ India . <p> In recent years , India has introduced policies to address resource shortages and waste management in the construction industry . Earlier , waste management rules ( 2000 ) focused only on municipal waste and did not cover construction and demolition waste ( C&amp;DW ) . As a result , informal workers handled most C&amp;DW recycling , collecting valuable materials like metals and bricks.To fix this , the C&amp;DW Management Rules ( 2016 ) provided clear waste segregation , treatment , and recycling guidelines . These rules required large cities to set up recycling plants and encouraged the use of recycled materials in government projects ( 10 -- 20% ) . Previously , Indian construction rules only allowed natural materials like sand and aggregates . @@126852536 <h> Opinion : Decolonising Indian Education -- Rethinking what we teach and why <p> India 's classrooms still carry echoes of a past that was n't entirely ours . Much of what we teach , and how we teach it , comes from an inherited script -- one that often places polished , distant knowledge above the messy wisdom of lived experience . For too long , education has privileged the abstract over the local , the universal over the particular . <h> Also Read <p> So , when we speak of decolonising education , it is not just about sprinkling folk tales into textbooks or renaming old institutions . It is about asking harder questions : Whose knowledge counts ? Whose voice shapes the syllabus ? And what kind of learners are we trying to create ? Decolonisation , at its core , is a quiet but radical act of reimagining what we value in our pursuit of learning . <p> Our Vedic and traditional knowledge needs a complete come-back and a warm acceptance . Indigenous knowledge systems are not just cultural footnotes ; they are living ways of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hinterlands , we still have those sky-gazing eyes of farmers who read the sky like a map , grandmothers who carry generations of healing in their wrinkled hands , and artisans whose work tells stories no textbook could hold . Their knowledge is not just beautiful -- it 's useful , especially in a world grappling with climate change , fragile ecosystems , and fractured communities . <p> One needs to pause , observe , listen , and feel to realise that achieving SDGs is actually not that difficult . However , they have been sidelined and long-dismissed as informal , non-academic , or simply not modern enough . A decolonised education does not add them in as an afterthought . It starts with them . It recognises that how we live , grow , and learn depends on whose knowledge we choose to honour . <p> From NEP to NCF : A Quiet Shift Gains Ground <p> The National Education Policy ( NEP ) 2020 rightly acknowledges the imbalance in our knowledge systems and calls for multilingual learning and culturally rooted teaching . However , policies do not change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the National Curriculum Framework ( NCF ) 2023 , which puts NEP 's ideas into motion . The NCF weaves Indigenous knowledge into subjects like environmental science , social studies , and ethics , ensuring students are harbouring the essence of their thought process . <p> The push for experiential , localised learning marks a move from symbolic gestures to pedagogical reorientation . What 's needed now is a sustained commitment to what may be called pedagogies of proximity -- approaches that shorten the cultural and cognitive distance between the learner and the curriculum . <p> These are not just methods but mindsets where education is embedded in place , language , and lived experience . Much still depends on the teacher 's capacity , curricular materials , and institutional support . The University Grants Commission ( UGC ) is putting rigorous efforts into this plan . The momentum is real but fragile . <p> Guard Against <p> These shifts are worth celebrating , but they call for care . Indigenous knowledge is not just a discourse -- it actually cuts through the thematic layers of regions , castes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ way to centre only on dominant traditions , we stand at a risk of trading one form of exclusion for another . <p> It 's not just about adding new content ; it 's about rethinking who delivers in the classroom , how and what , and whose voices shape the classroom . Are teachers free to draw from local wisdom ? Do students get to explore the knowledge rooted in their communities ? That 's where real change begins . Are oral traditions treated with the same seriousness as printed text ? These are the deeper questions we must address . <p> Decolonising education is n't about adding folk tales to textbooks or renaming institutions -- it 's about who gets to teach , what knowledge we prioritise , and whose voices shape the classroom <p> As India moves rapidly towards a Digital University ecosystem and AI-powered educational platforms , there is an opportunity -- and a lurking challenge . The question that arises is whether our digital education platforms can truly hold the richness of Indigenous knowledge or will they flatten it into standardised , searchable formats ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we do not just move to an online platform but also perpetuate spaces that are multilingual , interactive , and culturally rooted . <p> A Forward Agenda <p> To move decolonisation from policy to practice , a few grounded shifts are needed . First , we need translational pedagogies , spaces where community elders and teachers co-design lessons , especially in areas like environment , health , and local history . Second , schools should host local knowledge labs , where students document and share the traditions around them , turning learning into real civic engagement . <p> Third , teachers must be trained in epistemic pluralism -- learning how to teach diverse knowledge systems with care and academic rigour without romanticising or sidelining them . Fourth , open-access , multilingual platforms for Indigenous knowledge can make such resources accessible , respected , and widely used . <p> Finally , young people must be part of the process through projects like video ethnographies , crowdsourced glossaries , and innovation challenges rooted in their contexts . These steps can help make decolonisation not just a slogan but a living , inclusive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are n't about going backwards ; they 're about moving forward with deeper roots . In a world facing climate stress , mental health challenges , and a growing disconnect from the locals , a decolonised education offers more than cultural pride , it offers lived wisdom . NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 point us in the right direction , but the path ahead will need care , creativity , and collaboration . <p> The real question is n't whether Indigenous knowledge belongs in the classroom -- it 's whether our classrooms are ready to hold what that knowledge has to offer truly . Education is not just about transmitting knowledge but about reproducing society . The question is : whose society are we reproducing ? And if we must modernise , let it not be at the cost of memory . <p> After all , even Bourdieu would agree that habitus changes , but only when the field allows for new rules of the game . It 's time we updated the syllabus ... without uninstalling the soul . <p> ( The author is an Assistant Professor at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Hyderabad . Views are personal )

The statement has given a significant boost to Iran , the new joinee to the block in its foreign policy outreach after the attack on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It is also a reflection of changing geopolitical dynamics and a push back by developing countries to assert themselves . <p> What 's Brics ? <p> Brics initially referred to a group of nations undergoing swift economic expansion that , if sustained at comparable rates , would become the preeminent economic powers of the 21st century . The abbreviation , originating from the names of the initial members Brazil , Russia , India , China , and South Africa , has been adopted as the designation of a formal international organisation that seeks to enhance economic and geopolitical integration and cooperation among its member states . <p> The phrase Bric , representing Brazil , Russia , India , and China , was initially coined by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill to characterise the four economies that might potentially control the world economy by 2050 , if they sustain growth . Representatives of the BRIC nations commenced informal meetings during the 2006 session of the United Nations General Assembly ( UNGA ) , paving the way for the formalisation of the group in the future . <p> STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ BRIC nations reiterated their dedication to a multipolar world order and global non-interventionism , advocating for a new global reserve currency as a substitute for the U.S. dollar . In 2011 , South Africa became a member of the organisation , resulting in the group 's acronym being altered to Brics . This indicated a shift from a particular economic classification to a broader coalition of emerging regional leaders . <p> The Brics organisation is also perceived as an initiative to establish a geopolitical bloc that can counteract the dominance of Western-led global organisations like the International Monetary Fund ( IMF ) and the World Bank . The true cohesion and alignment of the Brics nations , as well as the actual worth of the alliance , however , remains a subject of contention . Several analysts highlight the significant disparities in the political systems , economy , and geopolitical standings of the member states as indicators of the organization 's fragility . <p> Brics expanded in 2024 to include Egypt , Ethiopia , Iran , and the UAE , with Indonesia joining in 2025 , along with ten associate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate financing , artificial intelligence governance , and alternative payment systems , while managing internal diversity and global issues . <p> STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD <p> About the 17th Brics Summit <p> The 17th Brics Summit took place in Rio de Janeiro , Brazil , on July 6-7 , 2025 , representing a significant event for the group during Brazil 's leadership , with the subject " Strengthening Global South Cooperation for More Inclusive and Sustainable Governance . " The Summit convened amid rising geopolitical tensions and a changing global order , seeking to establish Brics as a counterbalance to Western-dominated institutions such as the IMF and G7 , while steering clear of outright conflict . @@126874032 <p> In a world increasingly being shaped by rapid technological advancements , environmental crises , and deepening inequalities , the dominant models of quality education offer a narrow and inadequate vision . This paper makes a case for a multi-dimensional and adaptable capability approach ( CA ) that offers a transformative lens for guiding future policy reforms . It offers policy directions for India and other Global South contexts , advocating for a redefinition of quality indicators , contextualised curriculum reforms , strengthening teacher capabilities , embedding mental health and resilience , ensuring that digital capabilities are equitably nurtured , and deploying technologies such as artificial intelligence ethically for learner empowerment . The paper argues that adopting a CA lens is not only a philosophical shift but a practical policy requirement for creating just and resilient education ecosystems for human development . <h> Introduction <p> Since the 1950s , the word ' quality ' a has been used in the context of formal education and has become part of the critical discourse on structured and institutionalised learning . Concepts like ' reform ' , ' relevance ' , ' improvement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' innovation ' , signify an ongoing search for better practices and outcomes. 1 <p> In the discourse on quality education , the Capability Approach ( CA ) shifted the narrow focus on access or academic outcomes to the expansion of capabilities , freedoms , and individual well-being . It began to take shape in the 1980s and 1990s through the work of philosophers , Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum , and gained prominence beginning in the 21st century . Rather than asking how much learners know , CA asks what they are able to do or become with what they learn . Several emerging ideas in quality education -- such as competency-based education ( CBE ) , social-emotional development , and lifelong learning -- reflect CA 's influence . It has also shaped global frameworks like Sustainable Development Goal 4 ( UN 2030 Agenda ) , UNESCO 's Futures of Education ( 2021 ) and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development 's ( OECD ) Learning Compass 2030 . In India , the National Education Policy ( NEP ) 2020 resonates with CA and shifts the emphasis from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ National Curriculum Framework ( NCF ) 2023 takes on the task by emphasising play-based , enquiry-driven , and contextually meaningful learning that respects student agency . <p> This paper re-evaluates existing quality measures of education and proposes CA as a primary lens for the next decade of educational reform . It also focuses on how quality education can be reconceptualised and operationalised in policy to expand learners ' capabilities , agency , and dignity -- particularly amidst rapid global transformations such as the use of artificial intelligence , worsening climate crises , and widening inequalities . <p> The rest of the paper is structured into four sections . The first section provides a historical overview of how quality in education has been conceptualised across philosophical , economic , and pedagogical traditions -- from ancient times to the mid-20th century . It is followed by an examination of modern educational frameworks , focusing on the post-Second World War period , beginning with the Universal Declaration on Human Rights ( UDHR ) , 2 which marked the first global affirmation of education as a fundamental right , through to current deliberations on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ section describes two popular approaches to measuring quality -- human capital theory ( HCT ) and the humanistic model -- and outlines their critiques . It then introduces the capability approach , exploring its theoretical foundations , its redefinition of quality in more progressive ways , and its methodological contributions to measurement . The final main section presents recommendations and future directions , calling for a more learner-centric , equitable , and well-being-driven approach to defining and measuring quality education . <h> Historical Perspectives on Quality Education <p> In the ancient era , ' quality ' education was one that instilled moral virtue , civic responsibility , and philosophical intellect. 3 Plato ( 427 -- 347 BCE ) envisioned quality education as a means to build a just society , whereas Aristotle ( 384 -- 322 BCE ) articulated it as a tool to achieve human flourishing. 4 For both , education was not simply the attainment of theoretical knowledge but a " total training of character " where moral and intellectual development are central , along with a strong emphasis on dialectical reasoning and philosophical enquiry to build wisdom @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ early medieval period ( 5th -- 10th century ) , education was rooted in religious , cultural , and moral instruction , delivered through Christian monastic schools in Europe , Islamic madrasas in the Middle East , and Gurukuls or temple-based learning in South and Southeast Asia . Their curriculum included scriptural studies , theology , and sharing of traditional knowledge , often emphasising rote memorisation and strict adherence to religious doctrine , leaving little room for critical enquiry or intellectual exploration. 10 However , some centres of higher education ( like Takshshila and Nalanda ) were characterised by ' scholasticism ' -- i.e. , hard dialectical reasoning , which reconciled reason and faith. 11 <p> By the late medieval era , the Renaissance ( 13th -- 16th century ) marked a notable shift in Europe 's educational paradigm , moving away from purely religious instruction toward humanism and scientific enquiry . Thinkers such as Erasmus and Comenius advocated educational reform and proposed a liberal arts curriculum comprising grammar , logic , arithmetic , geometry , music , and astronomy. 12 Comenius was among the earliest to emphasise universal education @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , laying the groundwork for modern educational practices. 13 <p> Against this secular shift in Europe , East-Asian educational traditions saw a resurgence of spiritual and moral education . With the spread of Islam in the 13th century , madrasas became key institutions of learning , defining quality education through religious scholarship , linguistic proficiency ( especially in Arabic ) , and legal studies ( Sharia law ) . While some integrated subjects like astronomy and medicine , the dominant measure of quality remained the ability to interpret religious doctrine and apply moral reasoning. 14Top of Form <p> The Enlightenment ( 17th -- 18th century ) was a period of intellectual transformation that emphasised reason , empirical learning , and individual rights . Thinkers like Ren ? Descartes , John Locke , and Jean-Jacques Rousseau challenged rigid , traditional forms of learning and promoted approaches based on logic , experience , and intellectual autonomy . For example , Descartes introduced the idea that questioning , scepticism , and structured enquiry were essential to acquiring knowledge , 15 laying the foundation for scientific education that encouraged critical thinking over passive absorption. @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ human mind is shaped by experience and observation , 17 shifting education towards experiential learning -- later influencing hands-on , active engagement methods . Rousseau advocated a naturalistic approach to education , centred on exploration and direct engagement with surroundings. 18 , 19 Together , Enlightenment thinkers reshaped the understanding of quality education , moving away from memorising religious doctrines or applying moral reasoning to building a case for autonomy , critical thinking , and independent judgment. 20 <p> With the Industrial Revolution that began in the late 18th century , economies shifted from primarily agrarian activities to large-scale manufacturing , promoting a growing recognition of the need for a regulated education system to produce disciplined , obedient , and efficient workers . To develop these crucial qualities among industrial labour , institutionalised mass schooling emerged , featuring standardised curricula and a focus on efficiency and workforce preparation. 21 Educationists like Robert Owen , Andrew Bell , and Joseph Lancaster focused their efforts on education for working-class children , while in the United States , Horace Mann introduced public schooling . These thinkers believed that education ( particularly elementary education @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ state interests . Therefore , a high-quality education system was one that equipped individuals with workforce-ready skills , civic virtues , and responsible citizenship . They also supported government intervention ( through funding and legislation ) in education and built policy agendas where the state was concerned about the literacy , skills and quality of its children , i.e. , the future working population . It popularised the idea that education is a public good , crucial for the progress of a nation . While this democratised education and expanded its access , it also narrowed its focus. 22 , 23 <p> The early 20th century witnessed a shift towards learner-centred approaches , helped by advances in the domains of psychology , sociology , and pedagogy . These theories highlighted the importance of student agency , social interactions , and developmental needs in learning . John Dewey 's progressive education promoted experiential , democratic , and problem-solving-oriented learning. 24 Simultaneously , Lev Vygotsky emphasised the role of social interactions , arguing that learners achieved more with direction and collaboration than by themselves. 25 Jean Piaget provided insights on developmental stages @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with their cognitive abilities at different ages. 26 These insights transformed the understanding of educational quality , making it more dynamic , individualised , and student-centred . Adding to this , Paulo Freire 's critical pedagogy positioned education as a tool of empowerment and social transformation , encouraging students to develop critical consciousness and question power structures. 27 , 28 Together , these thinkers redefined quality education as a continuous endeavour that created independent thinkers , problem-solvers , and socially responsible individuals -- shifting the focus to process indicators like student agency , teaching methods , and interactive learning . <h> Modern Conceptualisations of Quality Education <p> After the Second World War , the concept of quality education was shaped by the global need for economic rebuilding , democratisation in newly independent nations , and the promotion of social cohesion through democratic ideals. 29 This period witnessed education becoming more centralised , solidifying the idea that mass schooling was necessary for national development. 30 Simultaneously , rising international aid , privatisation , and global competition led to a growing emphasis on learning outcomes , with standardised testing emerging as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some milestones in the discourse on quality education . <p> Table 1 : Milestones and Shifts in the Understanding of Quality Education Post-Second World War <p> The UDHR was the first global declaration of education as a fundamental human right ( Article 26 ) . Although not legally binding , it set an aspirational benchmark , framing education as a universal public good essential for individual and national development . Forty years later , the CRC established a legally binding framework , obligating states to provide free and compulsory primary education ( Article 28 ) and to improve access to secondary and higher education . <p> UNESCO 's 1996 Delors Report was a landmark in redefining education quality beyond basic literacy and numeracy . It introduced the " Four Pillars of Education " : <p> Learning to Know : developing skills for lifelong learning . <p> Learning to Do : developing technical and soft skills for employability . <p> Learning to Be : developing one 's full potential , as an independent , critical , responsible , and creative person . <p> Resting on these pillars , the Deloras Report @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , social , and intellectual development as integral to quality education . <p> In the 1980s , international aid and lending agencies such as the World Bank , SIDA ( Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency ) , and DFID ( Department for International Development ) influenced economic adjustments and planning in many developing countries. 43 They linked education to economic growth and productivity , encouraging governments to adopt market-driven curricula . Education quality was increasingly measured through indicators like enrolment , attendance , and literacy and numeracy outcomes. 44 , 45 <p> A more integrated , humanistic vision of education came with the SDGs ( 2015 ) , which emphasised " inclusive and equitable quality education " , and promoted CBE , digital literacy , and lifelong learning for adaptability in a rapidly changing world. 47 UNESCO 's Futures of Education initiative furthered it while advocating for sustainable , global , and peace-oriented education , responsive to technological and environmental shifts . Similarly , the OECD 's ' Future of Education and Skills 2030/2040 ' project and the ' OECD Learning Compass 2030 ' 48 emphasised transformative competencies ( knowledge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , adaptability , and well-being as cornerstones of quality education. 49 <p> School closures during the COVID-19 pandemic ( 2020-22 ) , which affected more than 1.6 million learners worldwide , 50 forced a global shift to online learning . This accelerated the use of AI , EdTech platforms , and hybrid education models . While technology expanded access , it also exposed inequalities , where the varying quality and effectiveness of remote learning led to an average learning loss of one-third to one-half of the year for students in less resourceful settings. 51 , 52 <p> The concept of quality education has evolved since the Second World War -- from basic access to a complex , multidimensional issue shaped by economic , social , technological , and individual factors . While global frameworks like the SDGs , CBE , SEL , and lifelong learning have redefined educational quality , persistent challenges in implementation and measurement remain . <h> Theories of Learning and Their Impact on Quality Discourse <p> Theories of learning have shaped perspectives on knowledge acquisition , the role of the teacher , and methods of assessing learning @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Cognitivism , Constructivism , Critical Pedagogy , and Connectivism -- and analyses their impact on contemporary debates on educational quality . of Quality of Education and Their Limitations <p> The rich discourse on quality education has rendered itself to many different @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ two models : the human capital or learning outcomes model , and the **28;1566;TOOLONG based measure . <p> Human Capital Theory ( HCT ) <p> The HCT model , championed by the World Bank , views education as an investment aimed at enhancing the skills and productivity of future workers , thereby increasing per-capita income and reducing unemployment . Quality education is often measured using metrics of learning outcomes , workforce skills , and economic returns . Through educational loans , pilot project funding , technical assistance , and other such pathways , the World Bank has influenced both international benchmarking and domestic evaluation policies across many countries. 62 Key examples include Programme for International Student Assessment ( PISA ) , Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study ( TIMSS ) , Progress in International Reading Literacy Study ( PIRLS ) and national assessments ( e.g. , the National Achievement Survey ( NAS ) in India ) . Besides learning outcomes , it relies on measuring returns of public and private spending on education for countries , income returns on education for individuals and skills mismatch analysis for the market-education @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , offer cross-country or inter-state comparisons , and track longitudinal trends , they primarily focus on academic and employability skills . This emphasis often overlooks the broader social , emotional , and civic aspects of education , neglecting creative abilities , learning experiences , and teaching methodologies. 63 They also do not capture individual , contextual , and structural factors affecting education quality. 64 Moreover , the theory presumes a direct , linear relationship between educational attainment and economic outcomes . However , this link may not be consistent , with many countries not realising the predicted gains in productivity despite expanding access and raising average years of schooling. 65 HCT also fails to account for structural inequalities that impact education and disregards the diverse ways in which education can empower individuals beyond labour market outcomes . This can perpetuate social stratification and reinforce existing power dynamics. 66 Therefore , as the world faces complex challenges like climate change , mental health crises , and technological disruption , the utilitarian logic of HCT appears increasingly outdated . <p> Humanistic Theory <p> In contrast , the humanistic theory of education , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of education . It considers a comprehensive framework encompassing five dimensions of quality -- context , inputs , teaching-learning processes , outputs , and outcomes -- to arrive at a holistic understanding of measuring and improving education quality . The figure below presents these dimensions , along with a list of indicators and their relationships . <p> Unlike standardised testing , this vision relies on mixed methods , including student engagement surveys , classroom observations , inspection reports , and self-evaluation for measuring quality . The framework has expanded to a futures perspective , with a focus on education that promotes lifelong learning and integrates social , cultural , and environmental aspects to address global challenges . In other words , quality education equips learners to navigate future complexities with a curriculum that includes ecological consciousness , global citizenship , digital literacy , and interdisciplinary knowledge. 68 <p> Scholars point out several practical problems in measuring education quality as per the humanistic visions , like time-intensiveness , resource demands , subjectivity in qualitative measurements , and difficulty in scaling these measures across diverse education systems. 69 Some also argue that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emphasise individualism , secularism , and rationality -- values that may not be relevant or culturally appropriate for many countries. 70 It therefore risks imposing a universalist framework that overlooks pluralistic and indigenous educational approaches . <p> While the two approaches may appear to be in conflict , a review of a cross-national dataset of 7,829 education reforms by Choi71 found that countries tend to adopt both in parallel rather than exclusively . In balancing economic needs with international commitments , policies often integrate both perspectives , ensuring education to serve the dual purpose of economic progress and social justice . <p> This interplay between HCT and humanistic perspectives aligns with the Capability Approach ( CA ) , which emphasises what individuals can actually do and be with their education . It emphasises agency , freedom and well-being -- capturing both the instrumental and intrinsic roles of education . <h> Perspectives from the Capability Approach <p> Besides inputs ( such as school enrolment ) , processes ( pedagogy ) , and outputs ( such as test scores ) , CA shifts the global discourse on quality education to actual capabilities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Capabilities refer to the real opportunities individuals have to achieve certain beings and doings , such as being educated or working , while ' functionings ' are the actual realisations of these capabilities , such as being literate or employed. 72 The distinction between capabilities ( means ) and functionings ( ends ) highlights that having resources is not sufficient ; people must also have the ability to convert these resources into achieved outcomes. 73 This conversion ability varies across individuals due to personal , social , and environmental factors. 74 <p> Therefore , as per CA 's conceptualisation , quality education should be measured by : <p> The capabilities it expands -- such as critical thinking , reasoning , and civic participation -- that individuals value ; and <p> The functionings it enables -- such as choices , agency , and well-being -- reflecting whether individuals have the freedom to convert their capabilities into meaningful life outcomes . <p> An educated person , therefore , is not merely someone who has passed exams or acquired degrees , but someone who has the freedom to pursue a life they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ marks a paradigm shift , influencing its understanding in seven specific ways : <p> Reframing Education as a Common Good : Before the conceptualisation of CA , education was classified as a public good , with emphasis on state provision and regulation . CA offers a ' common good ' perspective , recognising that education is not fully characterised by non-rivalry or non-excludability -- elite institutions , private schools , and tuition fees often create access barriers and reinforce inequalities. 75 This view challenges the assumption that access alone ensures equal opportunity and contends that education is not merely a state responsibility but a shared societal one . It must be actively protected and improved through collective participation and democratic governance. 76 <p> Education as Entitlement : Sen systematically refers to education as an entitlement . Unlike human rights , which are moral or legal claims , entitlements are shaped by social and institutional support and create enabling environments i.e. state capacity to provide funding , institutional support and social conditions for infrastructure , teacher training , and curriculum reforms . This perspective highlights that merely declaring education as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ educational capabilities into real-life skills. 77 <p> Education as a Process of Human Development : In CA , the goal of education is to further human development . It aligns with broader critiques of neoliberal educational policies and offers an alternative by shifting the focus from economic growth to economic purpose , with an emphasis on social justice . It promotes holistic individualism -- the idea that personal growth is inherently linked to socio-economic , cultural , and environmental contexts. 78 Quality education , therefore , does not stop at enhancing individual agency ; it must also foster collective capacities for democratic participation , social justice , and global cooperation . CA balances the protection of personal freedom and agency with a sense of communal responsibility , challenging both atomistic individualism and coercive collectivism . <p> Focus on Equal Capabilities : Departing from the emphasis on equal access , treatment , or outcomes , CA seeks quality education that ensures all learners have real , substantive opportunities to develop their capabilities and functionings. 79 This means enabling equal capabilities , along with favourable conversion factors -- such as inclusive social @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are necessary for flourishing. 80 While Sen does not prescribe a fixed list of capabilities , he advocates for their identification through deliberative , participatory processes that reflect contextual needs and priorities . Nussbaum , however , outlines a broader set of central capabilities that extend beyond economic productivity . Several of these -- such as the ability to reason , reflect , and innovate ; make life choices with practical reason ; play and be involved in artistic engagement , and have knowledge and skills to engage with political , social , and economic systems -- relate closely to education. 81 <p> Advocacy for Participatory , Context-Sensitive Education : CA challenges top-down , standardised models of quality education by advocating for participatory , context-sensitive frameworks that reflect local needs , values , and aspirations . Instead of imposing universal benchmarks , it emphasises deliberative and inclusive decision-making , ensuring that learners , educators , and local communities actively define what quality education should achieve in their specific contexts. 82 This adds dimensions like responsiveness to local needs , adaptability to local realities , and relevance for learners -- marking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Education for Future Freedom : While CA values individual choice and freedom , it makes an important exception for compulsory education . Sen frames education as a ' social opportunity ' and offers a ' future-oriented argument ' that extends beyond immediate benefits . While adults may freely shape their educational pathways , children lack the agency to make informed decisions about schooling. 84 Accordingly , rather than evaluating education solely through immediate indicators , CA argues that true educational quality lies in its lasting impact -- specifically , whether it expands an individual 's real freedoms , agency , and ability to lead a life they value long after schooling is over . This perspective shifts the focus from short-term academic achievement to a broader , lifelong view of education 's role in well-being and future freedoms . <p> Social Justice and Human Dignity : CA argues that education should be evaluated by its ability to enhance human dignity -- that is , the extent to which it allows learners to live with autonomy , respect , and self-worth. 85 This reorientation of the educational goal from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Within schools , the CA demands for inclusive , participatory learning environments that honour learners ' identities , backgrounds , and aspirations . Through quality education , it promotes personal empowerment and meaningful integration into society. 86 While Nussbaum agrees that human dignity is inherent , she contends that it still depends on the outer world for its full development . Therefore , dignity is a potentiality , which requires being implemented through a series of capabilities and functionings , which quality education must promote. 87 <h> Limitations and Challenges of CA <p> While CA is generally praised for its rich , human-centred perspective , its actual application in measuring quality education faces several challenges -- including difficulties in measurement , data limitations , resource intensiveness , and interdisciplinary complexities . <p> First , the approach includes qualitative ideas like agency , well-being , and dignity , which are difficult to operationalise and assess within a universally agreed framework . Several capabilities are multi-dimensional and context-specific , and therefore lack objective data collection methods . <p> Second , education policies prescribe standardised curricula and assessment models aimed at serving national @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aspirations , and personal agency poses a policy challenge . Besides , what people value may vary , depending on a host of personal and social factors . <p> Third , policies often rely on comparable metrics for educational reform , while the context-specific , qualitative indicators emphasised by CA make large-scale application infeasible . Expanding freedoms puts heavy demands on education , requiring financial , institutional , and human resources , which may be limited for a long-term commitment . Therefore , in the context of low-resource settings , CA 's abstract ideals often clash with local priorities , like basic literacy or vocational training , in many developing countries. 88 <p> These concerns have prompted Rawls to call it " an unworkable idea " , 89 while Roemer critiques it for being abstract and unspecified. 90 Therefore , the very flexibility that allows educators , policymakers , and communities to adapt CA to local contexts also limits its universal applicability . Moreover , with the growing adoption of digital and AI-supported education , algorithm-based datafication tends to reduce complex educational experiences to measurable outputs , often sidelining CA @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ AI system might flag a student as ' at risk ' based solely on low quiz scores , ignoring contextual factors like socioeconomic barriers or mental health struggles that CA would prioritise . Data silos and lack of interoperability also hinder the integration of qualitative insights with AI analytics. 91 <p> However , despite these limitations , CA is increasingly influencing international discourse on educational goals , policy frameworks , grassroots reforms , and assessment practices . Several evaluations are now adopting hybrid , mixed-methods approaches that combine objective data ( like test scores , attendance ) with subjective perspectives ( e.g. , student/teacher feedback and community engagement ) , like the Annual Status of Education Report ( ASER ) in India , the Young Lives Study in India , Ethiopia , Peru , and Vietnam , the Uwezo Learning Assessments in Kenya , Uganda , and Tanzania , the EduQUAL Study in South Africa , and the BRAC Education Programme in Bangladesh . <p> Therefore , even as CA offers an expansive and complex framework by encompassing a broad range of capabilities and functionings , and advancing ideals such @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- it may be nearly untenable to fully realise these ideals at any given time . Despite this , the pursuit itself remains both meaningful and necessary . Striving toward these ideals continues to drive progress and improvement , shaping educational policies , practices , and ethical commitments . The next section explores key initiatives and insights from various endeavours to apply CA to diverse educational contexts . <h> Applications of CA in Practice <p> The Capability Approach has supported diverse theoretical and empirical applications in education , allowing methodological innovations and context-specific adaptations while retaining its normative strength. 92 <p> Most notably , it has influenced several international frameworks -- such as UNDP 's Human Development Index , UNESCO 's SDG 4 , OECD 's Learning Compass 2030 , the World Economic Forum 's ( WEF ) Future of Jobs Report , as well as UNESCO 's Future of Education Initiative -- all of which promote a multidimensional view of education . These frameworks emphasise alternative measures that promote individual and collective well-being and prepare students for complex , uncertain futures ( see text box below ) . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ New Education Policy ( NEP ) of India that prioritises skills , practical application , and integrated learning over rote memorisation , and Finland 's ' future schools ' model , characterised by child well-being , holistic learning , and teacher-community collaboration . <p> Growing global concern about declining child well-being -- particularly in mental health -- has shifted perceptions of educational goals , as this trend poses a serious threat to young people 's prospects and productivity , 93 International benchmark-setters like UNESCO and OECD are increasingly shifting student well-being and human flourishing alongside academic goals . Recognising this shift , PISA expanded its scope in 2015 to include indicators like students ' sense of belonging and self-efficacy . Its **25;1596;TOOLONG model now integrates well-being indicators alongside educational and economic outcomes , emphasising that experiences , perceptions , and contextual factors are crucial to student success. 94 Looking ahead , both UNESCO and OECD envision education as a means of human flourishing . They highlight that high-performing education systems of the future will be defined by four key principles : broader capabilities , ethical leadership , sustainable development , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Second , CA has been employed in ethnographic studies , non-normative research , and the assessment of educational projects . Under its influence , they have shown significant findings , like how communities perceive education and well-being and the non-economic returns of education , including improved participation , decision-making , and self-confidence. 97 , 98 , 99 For example , Alkire assessed the impact of an Oxfam literacy project for women in Pakistan using CA . Her finding revealed that the outcomes went beyond literacy gains to include enhanced confidence , awareness , and strengthened social networks . This underscored the intrinsic value of expanded capabilities in enhancing individual well-being and agency . <p> Third , CA has been leveraged to assess capability and functioning deprivation among marginalised groups of children . Educational strategies informed by CA have been particularly influential in the education of marginalised children and those with special needs , where the approach helps balance individualised support with broader goals of social inclusion. 100 The following case study illustrates how CA has been applied to assess education for girls in India , Bangladesh , and South @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ schools in Delhi applied CA principles to study hidden curriculum and its differential impact on boys and girls . The data showed that pervasive sexism in co-educational setting privileged boys , particularly through unequal classroom participation. 101 Boys received 15 percent more teacher interactions , while girls accounted for only 33 percent of academic interaction but 65 percent of conduct-related interaction . Self-reports revealed that only 21.3 percent girls felt comfortable asking a query in class , as against 32 percent boys . By Grade 5 , this disparity had already influenced stereotypical subject choices , preferences in games and activities , preferences , aspirations , and self-beliefs . The study concluded that while education may build instrumental capacities such as qualifications and degrees , it may limit equal development of intrinsic capacities -- like capacity to play , express oneself , and participate . Schooling , therefore , is not a linear process of enhancing capacities ( as against qualifications and degrees ) but a process laced with many complexities and challenges . <p> Bangladesh : Bangladesh displayed impressive quantitative progress in female literacy with rising enrolment rates and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ensure equal access to primary and secondary education for boys and girls by 2005 . In this context -- where official claims that gender disparity has been eliminated -- Raynor assessed gender equality in Bangladesh schools using CA and concluded that there were large gaps in attendance , achievement , and outcomes of education . She concluded , " claims relate to the target of eliminating gender disparity in education rather than the goal of promoting gender equality and empowering women . Therefore , even if the target has been reached , the goal has not " . 102 In another study , an evaluation of the BRAC 's non-formal Adolescent Development Programme based on Nussbaum 's list of capabilities , it found that while education ( including life skills education ) developed girls ' capabilities of : 1 ) practical reason 2 ) senses , imagination , and thought , 3 ) affiliation ; and 4 ) life , bodily health , and bodily integrity ; it did not enhance their agency , as they lacked control over their environments . While Raynor challenges the notion of education as a universal capability and questions the indivisibility of capabilities , she concludes that Nussbaum 's list is a useful framework for identifying which capabilities are flourishing and which are failing through education . <p> South Africa : In 2003 , Unterhalter critically examined CA in the context of South African education , particularly concerning gender inequalities and the HIV/AIDS epidemic. 103 She distinguished education from schooling and argued that while education could always enhance human capability , it might not always be the case with schooling -- arguably and certainly , schooling should expand the agency and freedom of young people . Schooling occurs in complex social contexts , where factors such as gender and racial inequality , along with prevalent issues like sexual harassment , can hinder the realisation of capabilities . National statistics on enrolment ratios , gender parity indices , and pass percentages suggested that girls were doing well in South African education . These data provided important , but only preliminary information to measure education capabilities . In reality , Unterhalter found that girls ' independence was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agency , and aspirations were not adequately protected or nurtured . She concluded that if schooling does not promote essential capabilities like practical reason , affiliation , bodily integrity and health -- it can not be termed as quality education . <p> Fourth , CA has influenced teacher education to focus on expanding teachers ' capacities . For example , in the Rhodes University B.Ed . ( Foundation Phase ) programme , CA principles were used to design training courses that prioritised teacher well-being , agency , and the ability to convert educational inputs into meaningful teaching practices . The programme aimed to ensure that future educators were not just trained in technical competencies but were also equipped with critical thinking , decision-making , and social awareness skills to apply contextually responsive teaching. 104 Similarly , a school intervention programme in Tanzania showed improvements in teacher agency and well-being. 105 <p> Fifth , CA has influenced various aspects of education -- from course designs to assessments , at all levels , from pre-school to university . Examples include Margaret Carr 's Learning Stories in early education , 106 Holistic Progress @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stage education in India ; 107 and the self-selected , self-directed elective courses offered at the University of Edinburgh. 108 <p> Collectively , these efforts demonstrate the versatility of CA in educational research and practice . By focusing on individual freedoms and the actual opportunities available to learners , CA provides a robust framework for analysing and addressing educational inequalities , informing policy development , and enhancing educational practices across various contexts . <h> Recommendations and Conclusion <p> This paper argues that CA offers a necessary framework for rethinking quality education from a more holistic , inclusive , and justice-oriented lens . It centres education as the expansion of capabilities and real freedoms and identifies four new frontiers to rethink quality education . <p> First , quality education should afford real freedoms -- learning environments must support conversion factors that allow students to translate skills and mindsets into real-world success . Second , it must be locally defined , acknowledging learners ' diverse historical , social , economic , and linguistic contexts . This approach creates space for indigenous knowledge systems , community-based learning , and participatory assessments . Third @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ future-readiness , adaptability , and agency . It also urges policies to support continuous education through reskilling programmes , adult education , and open-access learning platforms . Last , it must centre human dignity , agency , and well-being -- addressing social inequalities alongside workforce preparation and skill development . Key recommendations for strengthening and future-proofing education from the CA perspective , particularly for India , include : <p> Redefine Quality Education Beyond Measurable Outcomes : Move from a narrow , outcomes-based model to one aligned with frameworks like OECD 's Better Life Index , or UNESCO 's happy schools or quality-of-life models . These emphasise education 's impact on agency , well-being , civic participation , and future readiness . While applied to some extent in the Global North , they require contextualisation for the Global South . India could pilot a " Quality of Life through Education Index " ( QLEI ) across select aspirational districts , with domains like Agency ( student participation , opportunities for self-directed learning ) , Well-being ( mental health support , positive teacher-student relations ) , Civic Participation ( involvement in community @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ skills , digital capabilities , and green skills ) . The index should be implemented through participatory design and assessed using mixed methods , including self-assessment , peer feedback , and teacher observations . <p> Contextualised Curriculum and Assessment Systems : NCERT ( National Council of Educational Research and Training ) , with SCERTs ( State Council of Educational Research and Training ) and DIETs ( District Institute of Education and Training ) , should co-create contextualised curricula and assessment rubrics . In tribal regions like Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh , for example , curricula can incorporate local history , culture , and traditions while aligning with national objectives . Assessments should blend standardised metrics with adaptable indicators like reflective essays , peer-reviewed presentations , and qualitative indicators like reasoning , reflection or agency . While India 's recently launched holistic progress report cards mark a shift toward comprehensive assessments , they need to be expanded to measure a broader spectrum of capabilities , as well as to cover higher grades with age-appropriate indicators . <p> Strengthen Teacher Agency : Teachers should not be seen merely as transmitters of knowledge , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Their agency can be enhanced by : <p> Identifying a list of capabilities for teachers and aligning their continuous professional development ( CPD ) that include modules on well-being , inclusion , leadership , and ethical decision-making . <p> Institutionalising teacher voice through local and state-level platforms that enable teachers to influence policy , curriculum , and assessment design . <p> To achieve these , there is an urgent need to expand and diversify the pool of mentor teachers under the National Mission for Mentoring ( NMM ) . 109 The NMM portal must be enhanced for seamless interactions , resource sharing and progress tracking . <p> Bridge the Digital Divide with a Capability Lens : Efforts to bridge the digital divide in education must promote equitable and meaningful access for all learners -- like voice-based tools for early readers , disability-accessible apps , or vocational content for rural youth . Digital literacy should not be built as a skill , but as a capability . This means going beyond technical proficiency to fostering digital confidence , critical content evaluation , self-expression , and the use of technology to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Expand Access to Special Schemes with a Focus on Improving Functionings : Facilities like Atal Tinkering Labs ( ATLs ) under Atal Innovation Mission ( 2016 ) and Smart Classrooms Samagra Shiksha ( 2018 ) often remain limited to well-resourced institutions , bypassing the broader student population . Instead , it advocates for education that fosters ethical reflection , collective action , and a global responsibility. 110 Capabilities such as adaptability , critical thinking , problem-solving , and civic participation are essential for enabling learners to shape environmental policies rather than passively adapt to climate crises . These can be honed through project-based learning , community action projects and climate club activities in schools that foster civic engagement and leadership . <p> Strengthen CA in AI-Driven Education Reforms : As digital and AI-supported learning becomes central to education systems , it is critical to evaluate such transformations through the lens of CA . AI tools must be deployed not merely for efficiency of learning outcomes , but to enhance human agency , holistic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pedagogical empowerment of both learners and teachers and the inclusion of AI ethics and adaptive mindsets as foundational capabilities . Therefore , it supports the integration of modules on data ethics , privacy , and responsible use in school curriculum for both teachers and students . UNESCO 's ethical AI competency frameworks should be contextualised for India through a structured , inclusive , and iterative process involving key stakeholder groups and leveraging both global guidance and local realities . CA ideas can be helpful in the assessment of long-term impacts of technology on learners ' freedoms , creativity , and civic participation , besides the short-term engagement metrics . <p> The Capability Approach ensures that education remains a means of expanding freedoms rather than just fulfilling economic , technological , or survival-based imperatives . An increase in disposable income will further push the per capita fish consumption , which needs to be considered to accurately project the demand growth in the coming years . With 90% of the state 's population consuming fish , an increase in population naturally pushes up the fish demand , and the state becoming self-reliant to meet this demand is vital for its economy and reduces dependence on supplies from other states . Rising fish consumption puts pressure on inland fisheries and increases the risk of overexploitation of fish stock in natural water bodies . Diversion of forest for infrastructure projects such as expansion of highways , construction of greenfield highways , expansion of railway lines , and laying of new tracks results in fragmentation of the forest patches in protected areas and adverse impact on the ecology of rivers and streams . The rising atmospheric temperature and extreme weather events have given rise to conservation threats to the natural waterbodies and their ecology , which calls for mitigation measures to conserve indigenous and endangered fish species . The strategy for increasing production to prevent overexploitation in natural waterbodies such as wetlands , rivers , and lakes is to promote aquaculture through controlled cultivation in ponds and tanks and rearing fish in floating enclosures placed in rivers , lakes , etc . As the Earth 's average temperature rises due to increased greenhouse gas concentrations , the atmosphere can contain around 7% more water vapour every degree Celsius increase . While the concept is not new , it takes on fresh urgency in the context of ongoing India-EU FTA negotiations . With a mutually agreed timeline of finalising the deal by end-2025 , this is an opportune moment to examine potential implications of CBAM for India 's merchandise trade and manufacturing - and how policy could possibly turn this challenge into an opportunity for growth , development and green jobs . <p> From January @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ full compliance and carbon costs on six carbon-intensive imports : iron and steel , aluminium , electricity , cement , fertilisers , and hydrogen . It is , therefore , viewed as a serious non-tariff barrier for India . <p> While the official objective is to eliminate the cost advantage that foreign producers enjoy over EU-based green manufacturers , the measure will increase the cost of imports from developing countries while generating significant revenue for the EU . <p> India has raised concerns about CBAM , advocating for exemptions - especially for MSMEs - and calling for more equitable alternatives @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ time , FTA is important for India , offering access to the EU 's 27-member market of nearly 450 mn consumers . Key sectors like textiles , leather , pharmaceuticals , automobiles , IT services and agriculture are expected to benefit from increased exports . European companies are expected to invest in manufacturing linkages , fostering ancillary industries and joint ventures - particularly with MSMEs . India-EU cooperation on climate goals could also contribute to global progress toward net-zero targets . <p> But India and other developing countries view CBAM as WTO-incompatible and unfair , especially as the EU 's methodology for calculating embedded emissions remains under scrutiny . It must also establish a domestic carbon-pricing mechanism to assign a financial value to the carbon content of goods . With the EU recently considering carbon credits from overseas projects as part of its climate strategy , India could tap into this opportunity - once institutional mechanisms for pricing and trading carbon emissions are in place . <p> A long-term strategy is essential for a successful green transition , which will hinge on access to advanced technologies , climate finance and incentives for the private sector to adopt clean energy , and produce green steel , cement and other materials . <p> Meanwhile , one suggestion to neutralise CBAM is to introduce a domestic carbon tax that could be offset against the EU 's CBAM under a double-taxation avoidance framework . @@126892966 <h> Plant fossils , Karewas and climate change : A story of another Kashmir <p> ( Photo used for representative purposes only ) The Kapran village in South Kashmir 's Anantnag district Reuters <p> With its snowy winters and dry summers , Kashmir 's climate differs from rest of the country . Once upon a time , however , it too had a warm monsoon climate . A new study reveals how rising mountains changed all that -- shaping the region 's weather , landscape , and ecology . <p> Researchers from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences ( an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Science and Technology ) , and the University of Kashmir analysed fossilised leaves from ancient lake bed sediments in South Kashmir . These sediments , known as the Karewas , hold vital clues to the Valley 's climatic history . <p> For the uninitiated , the Karewas are thick deposits of clay , sand , silt and gravel found across the Kashmir Valley . Formed over millions of years , these layers were laid down in an ancient lake that once covered much of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rich in fossils , but also crucial for agriculture , supporting crops like saffron and apples . <p> The study was conducted as part of the rich fossil leaf collection curated by the late Professor Birbal Sahni and Dr G.S . Puri , which is housed at the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences ( BSIP ) , Lucknow : collections recovered from the Karewa sediments . <p> These displayed remarkable diversity and preservation . Many of the specimens resembled subtropical taxa that no longer exist in the region 's current temperate climate . <p> A group of researchers from BSIP were intrigued by the striking mismatch between past and present vegetation , and this prompted their scientific investigation into the climatic and tectonic history of the Kashmir Valley using modern palaeobotanical methodologies . <p> By studying leaf fossils from the Lower Karewa formations , scientists reconstructed what the climate was like around 3 -- 4 million years ago , during the late Pliocene period . <p> The study done by Harshita Bhatia , Reyaz Ahmad Dar and Gaurav Srivastava revealed that earlier , the average annual temperature was around 18 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 9 -- 10 month growing season . The rainfall was heavy in summer , driven by monsoon winds , while winters were relatively dry . This high moisture levels and humidity suggested a lush , subtropical environment . <p> These conditions are radically different from today 's Mediterranean-type climate in Kashmir , where most rain comes in winter via the Western Disturbances . <p> The authors linked this dramatic shift to the tectonic uplift of the Pir Panjal Range , a sub-Himalayan Mountain range that gradually rose and blocked the Indian summer monsoon from reaching the valley . Around four million years ago , tectonic activity began pushing these mountains higher , eventually blocking the summer monsoon winds from entering the valley . <p> With its main source of rainfall cut off , Kashmir 's climate began transitioning into what we see today : cold winters , dry summers , and winter precipitation from the west . Over milennia , these rising mountains cut off the water supply , drying out the lush forests and transforming the region 's climate from subtropical to Mediterranean . <p> Using CLAMP ( Climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shape , size and margins of fossil leaves to determine temperature and rainfall patterns , and cross-checked plant fossils with their modern relatives , using the help of the co-existence approach to estimate climate ranges . This helped them create a detailed snapshot of the Kashmir Valley 's ancient environment , rich with warmth and rain -- until the mountains intervened . <p> The research offers a window into how landscapes and climates evolve in response to tectonic shifts . It also helps explain the region 's rich biodiversity , preserved in the fossil record of the Karewas . <p> The study , published in the journal ' Palaeogeography , Palaeoclimatology , Palaeoecology ' , highlights how geological processes like mountain-building can trigger major climate changes over time . <p> The lead author say that the findings could improve our understanding of past climate systems and how future environmental changes might unfold -- especially in fragile mountain regions like the Himalayas .
